newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania says rating is vote of confidence.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania says rating is vote of confidence.

text.p: Lithuania said on Thursday that its credit rating from Moody's Investors Service was a vote of confidence in its reforms and would help attract investment needed to complete its transition to a market economy.

Moody's, a New York-based credit rating agency, on Wednesday assigned a Ba2 rating to Lithuania's foreign currency debt and a Ba3 to the country's bank deposits. It is the first credit rating granted to a former Soviet republic.

"This is a vote of confidence in Lithuania's reforms...the international business and financial community is recognizing the success of Lithuania's economic strategies," Algis Avizienis, general director of the Lithuanian Investment Agency, told Reuters.
He added that the rating showed foreign investors expected the reform process to continue after October's parliamentary elections.
The ruling Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party is expected to be replaced by a centre-right coalition at the polls.
"All of the major parties in the election are pro-reform," Avizienis said.
Lithuania has successfully pursued an IMF-sponsored programme of macro-economic reform which has reigned in inflation and kept its debt load down.
Moody's backed its rating by pointing to Lithuania's low external debt burden, the success of its budget stabilisation policies and the pro-reform attitude of its major parties.

But Moody's noted that much work needs to be done in key areas such as the heavily endebted and inefficient energy sector and the banking industry, which remains undercapitalised and burdened by non-performing loans.
The country is still recovering from the affects of a banking crisis which broke late last year with the surprise closure of two of its top banks.
Avizienis said the rating should attract badly needed foreign investment, an area where Lithuania is seen as lagging behind Baltic sibling Estonia.
"The rating should attract increased foreign attention to our treasury bill and equity markets," said Arvydas Acikevicius, manager of the trading department in the Lithuanian brokerage house Suprema.
The foreign share of Lithuania's domestic T-bill market is currently 40 percent.
U.S. investment bank Merril Lynch has underwritten a 200 million litas bond issue for the country, with an annual coupon of 20.125 percent.
The country made its debut on the international capital markets last year with a $60 million Eurobond with a two-year maturity and a 10 percent coupon.
"The rating will increase our options and reduce our borrowing costs in the future," a senior finance ministry official said.
U.S. analysts said that given Lithuania's modest borrowing needs they did not expect the country to bring much paper before the international capital markets.
